title: STENDEC
subtitle: Star Dust's last word · the Andes, 1947
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Desaturated documentary still, August 1947, the high snow-covered Andes in deep winter, heavy grey cloud and blowing snow, cold blue-grey light with faint warm brass tones, period 1940s detail, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic wide composition, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no lettering, no signage, no people, no faces.

beats.vo: Over the Andes, nineteen forty-seven. The airliner Star Dust sent its last message in Morse code. It ended in a word that has never been explained.
beats.img: A single brass Morse telegraph key mounted on a worn wooden radio operator's desk inside a 1940s piston airliner, centred and sharply lit by a small warm lamp, a bulky valve radio set with round dials behind it, a small cockpit window beyond showing grey cloud and snowy mountain peaks, still and silent.

beats.vo: S. T. E. N. D. E. C. The operator in Santiago asked again. The same word came back, twice more.
beats.img: A 1940s airfield radio room at dusk, a large valve radio receiver with glowing dials and a pair of headphones resting on a desk beside a blank paper message pad and a pencil, a window behind showing distant snow-covered Andes peaks under heavy cloud, empty chair, no people.

beats.vo: Star Dust never arrived. In nineteen ninety-eight, climbers found its wreckage high on Mount Tupungato.
beats.img: A single weathered aircraft propeller blade and a corroded piece of an old aluminium engine cowling half-buried in glacier ice and snow, high on a vast snowy mountain slope under a grey sky, no people.

beats.vo: The crash is broadly understood: in thick cloud, the crew descended too soon. No one aboard survived.
beats.img: A towering snow-covered Andes peak almost hidden inside dense grey cloud and blowing snow, seen from high in the air, a faint pale gap in the cloud, cold and silent, no aircraft visible.

beats.vo: The word is not. A scrambled 'descent'? A misheard Morse sign-off? Only theories, never confirmed.
beats.img: The same brass Morse key on an empty wooden desk in near darkness, a single thin beam of cold light falling across it, a dark window behind with faint snowy mountain shapes in cloud, quiet and unresolved.

facts.claim: Star Dust (BSAA Avro Lancastrian G-AGWH), Buenos Aires to Santiago, lost over the Andes on 2 August 1947; 11 aboard (6 passengers, 5 crew), all died
Final Morse message sent 17:41, 'ETA SANTIAGO 17.45 HRS STENDEC' (four minutes before planned arrival), received by the radio operator at Santiago (Los Cerrillos) — NOT Mendoza

The operator did not recognise the word and asked for clarification/repeat; the same word came back twice more (three receptions total). Wikipedia: 'repeated twice in succession'; Horizon/NOVA transcript: 'repeated again twice'
Star Dust never arrived; wreckage (Rolls-Royce engine) found by two Argentine climbers on Mount Tupungato in 1998; Argentine Army expedition 2000; DNA identifications by 2002

Crash broadly understood: 2000 Argentine investigation attributed it to snowstorm/heavy cloud preventing position correction; Horizon/NOVA: crew began descent in cloud believing they were near Santiago (jet-stream headwind), still short of Tupungato — controlled flight into terrain

Meaning of STENDEC has never been definitively explained; theories include an anagram of 'DESCENT' and Morse misreadings (e.g. spacing error around the AR sign-off / SCTI AR); none confirmed. Horizon: 'a final riddle which science has been unable to solve'
